turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My partner's been on my case about something. I don't really see what the big deal is. I'm fine, I can handle it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like there’s some tension in your relationship right now, and even if you don’t see it as a big issue, it’s clearly bothering your partner. Sometimes when we feel like we’re "handling it," we might dismiss our own emotions or theirs without realizing it.

Can you tell me more about what they’ve been bringing up? How does it make you feel when they do? Even if the issue itself doesn’t seem major to you, the fact that it’s causing friction might be worth exploring.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Look, I just think they're being too uptight. I like to unwind after work, that's all. I'm not hurting anyone. And yeah, they get a bit mad when they find out, but I just tell 'em I'm fine, that I can stop anytime. I don't see why it's such a problem.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you’re feeling a bit defensive because you don’t see your way of unwinding as harmful—it’s your time to relax, and you don’t want that taken away. At the same time, your partner’s reactions suggest they’re worried about something deeper, even if you don’t share that concern.

When you say you can "stop anytime," does that feel true to you? Or is there a part of you that might wonder if it’s harder than you’re letting on? And when your partner gets upset, what do you think they’re really afraid of? Sometimes the conflict isn’t just about the behavior itself, but what it represents to them—like feeling disconnected or worried about your well-being.

Would you be open to exploring what’s underneath their reactions, even if you don’t agree with them? It might help you both feel heard.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (scoffs slightly) Oh, come on, I don't know why they're making such a big deal out of this. I can stop anytime, like I said. But, I guess...I mean, I've tried to cut back before, and it's just really hard. It's like my head starts spinning and I feel...off. Not good. And yeah, maybe my partner's worried about me, but I'm fine. I'm fine, right? (crosses arms, looking slightly uncomfortable)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that—it takes courage to acknowledge that it might not be as simple as you initially thought. It sounds like there’s a part of you that knows this isn’t just about relaxing, but also about how hard it is to step away from it, even when you want to. That discomfort you’re describing—feeling "off" or like your head is spinning—those are real experiences, and they’re worth paying attention to.

You’re asking if you’re fine, and I hear the uncertainty in that. What does "fine" look like to you? Is it just about being able to function, or is there more to it, like feeling at peace or connected to the people you care about? Your partner’s worry might be coming from a place of love, even if the way they’re expressing it isn’t landing well with you. They might be seeing something you’re not fully acknowledging yet.

Would it be okay if we explored what’s happening for you when you try to cut back? What’s that "off" feeling about, and what does it tell you about what you might need? You don’t have to have all the answers right now—just being open to looking at it is a big step.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks away, fidgeting slightly) Yeah, okay...fine's just...not being a mess, I guess. Not feeling like I'm losing control or anything. (pauses, then looks back) And, to be honest, when I try to cut back, it's like my whole body aches or something. I feel restless, irritable...just on edge. And mornings are the worst. I wake up feeling like...like I've been hit by a truck or something. It's like my whole system is just...shut down, you know? (looks down, rubbing the back of neck)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that with me—it’s not easy to talk about feeling that kind of physical and emotional discomfort. What you’re describing—aches, restlessness, irritability, feeling like your system is shut down—those are classic signs of withdrawal, and they’re your body’s way of telling you that it’s become dependent on whatever you’re using to unwind. That’s not a failure on your part; it’s just how your brain and body adapt when something becomes a regular part of your routine, especially if it’s been used to cope with stress or emotions.

It sounds like part of you is frustrated because you don’t *want* to feel this way—you want to be in control, to feel like you’re not "a mess." But right now, your body is telling you that it’s struggling to function without this thing, and that’s creating a real internal conflict for you. You’re caught between wanting to feel "fine" and feeling like you’re not quite there yet.

I’m also hearing that mornings are particularly hard for you. What’s that like emotionally? Does it feel overwhelming, or does it make you feel guilty or anxious about the day ahead? And how does this all tie into your relationship with your partner? Do you think they’re picking up on some of these struggles, even if you’re trying to downplay them?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, rubbing hands together) Yeah, mornings are...tough. It's like, I'll wake up and I'll feel this...this dread, I guess. Like, I know I'm gonna be okay, but it's hard to get out of bed. And then I'll start thinking about all the things I gotta do, and it just feels like...like too much. (pauses, taking a deep breath) And, yeah, I'm sure my partner's picked up on it. They're always on my case about getting up earlier, being more productive...like, I know I should be doing better, but it's hard when I'm feeling like this. (looks up, a hint of defensiveness creeping in) And it's not like I'm just being lazy or anything. I'm trying, okay? But it's just...hard.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I hear you—mornings sound like they’re carrying a lot of weight for you, and that dread isn’t just about the day ahead. It’s like your body and mind are already bracing for a battle before you’ve even gotten out of bed. That’s exhausting, and it makes sense that it would feel like "too much." You’re not lazy; you’re dealing with something that’s making even small tasks feel overwhelming.

And when your partner pushes you to "do better," it probably feels like they’re not seeing how hard you’re already trying. That disconnect can make you feel even more alone in this, like you’re failing at something that should be simple. But what if this isn’t about productivity or willpower? What if it’s about your body and mind being stuck in a cycle that’s harder to break than it seems?

You mentioned earlier that cutting back feels impossible because of the physical and emotional fallout. That’s not a lack of effort—it’s a sign that this has become more than just a habit. It’s something your system now *needs* to function, even if it’s causing problems in other areas of your life. That’s a really tough spot to be in, and it’s okay to admit that it’s not as easy as just "stopping."

Would it help to explore what this cycle looks like for you? Not to judge it, but to understand it better—like mapping out what happens before, during, and after you use, and how it connects to these morning struggles? That might give us some clues about where to start making changes that actually feel manageable.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (looks down, nodding slightly) Yeah, that might help. I mean, it's just...it's like, I'll start using in the evening, and it'll help me wind down, you know? But then when I try to stop, it's like my body just...rebels, I guess. It's hard to sleep, I get restless, and like I said, the mornings are the worst. And even when I'm not using, I can still feel this...this tension, like my body's just waiting for the next fix. (pauses, looking up) It's hard to explain, but it's like I'm stuck in this perpetual state of...of needing something, you know? Like, I'm not even sure what I'm looking for, but I know it's not just relaxation or fun. It's something deeper than that. (shakes head) And I don't know how to break out of it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Thank you for sharing that—it takes real courage to put words to something that feels so overwhelming and confusing. What you’re describing is more than just a habit; it’s a cycle that’s hijacked your body’s natural rhythms, and it’s left you feeling like you’re constantly chasing something that never quite satisfies. That "tension" you’re talking about—that’s your nervous system stuck in a state of anticipation, like it’s always bracing for the next hit, the next moment of relief. It’s exhausting, and it makes sense that you’d feel trapped in it.

You’re right that this isn’t just about relaxation or fun. When something becomes this all-consuming, it’s often filling a void or soothing a discomfort that’s deeper than we realize. Maybe it’s numbing stress, loneliness, or even a sense of emptiness that’s hard to name. The fact that you’re aware of this—that you can feel the difference between what you *think* you’re getting and what you’re *actually* getting—is a really important step. It means there’s a part of you that knows this isn’t working, even if the rest of you feels stuck.

Breaking out of this cycle isn’t about willpower or just "trying harder." It’s about rewiring your brain and body to find other ways to cope with that underlying tension. That might mean exploring what’s driving the need to "fix" in the first place—whether it’s stress, trauma, or just the weight of daily life. It might also mean finding small, manageable ways to interrupt the cycle, like replacing one habit with another or learning to tolerate the discomfort of withdrawal with support.

Would it be okay if we started by exploring what that "something deeper" might be? What do you think you’re really looking for when you reach for this? And what would it look like to give yourself even a little bit of that in a healthier way? You don’t have to have all the answers—just being open to the question is a start.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, taking a deep breath) Yeah, okay...I think I'm looking for a way to escape, I guess. Not just from the present moment, but from my own thoughts and feelings. It's like, when I'm using, I can just...tune out, you know? Forget about everything that's been bothering me. But when I'm not using...I'm just left with all these thoughts and feelings, and it's overwhelming. (pauses, looking up) And I don't know how to deal with them. I feel like I'm just...stuck in my own head, and I don't know how to get out.

(sighs, rubbing hands together) It's like, I'm scared to feel all these things, because they're so...intense. And I don't know how to handle them. So I just...numb myself, I guess. And it's not working, because I'm still feeling all these things underneath. (looks down, shaking head) I don't know, it just feels like I'm stuck in this cycle, and I don't know how to break free.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
What you’re describing is so much more common than people realize—this feeling of being trapped in your own mind, where emotions and thoughts feel like too much to handle, so numbing becomes the only way to cope. It’s like your brain has learned that the only way to survive the overwhelm is to check out, even if it’s just for a little while. But the problem is, the feelings don’t actually go away; they just get buried, and then they come back even louder when the numbing wears off. It’s a cycle that leaves you feeling stuck, like you’re running in place but never getting anywhere.

You said you’re scared to feel these things because they’re so intense. That fear makes a lot of sense—when emotions feel big and unmanageable, it’s natural to want to avoid them. But here’s the thing: what if the intensity isn’t the problem? What if the problem is that you’ve never had the tools or the support to *be with* those feelings in a way that doesn’t feel so overwhelming? Numbing works in the short term, but it also robs you of the chance to learn that you *can* handle these emotions, even if it’s uncomfortable at first.

Breaking free from this cycle isn’t about stopping the numbing and suddenly being okay with feeling everything all at once. It’s about learning to approach those feelings in small, manageable doses, with support. It’s about giving yourself permission to feel *some* of it, without letting it consume you. For example, if anxiety or sadness feels like a tidal wave, maybe we start by just dipping a toe in the water—acknowledging the feeling without letting it pull you under.

Would it help to explore what some of those overwhelming feelings are? Not to dive into them all at once, but to name them, so they feel a little less scary? And what would it look like to give yourself a little bit of what you’re really needing—maybe not escape, but a way to feel safe or grounded, even when the feelings are intense? You don’t have to do this alone. We can take it one step at a time.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, taking a deep breath) Okay...I think I'm scared of feeling anxious and overwhelmed. It's like, my mind just goes racing and I feel like I'm going to freak out or something. And I'm scared of feeling sad, because it feels so...heavy. Like, it's just this big weight that I don't know how to carry.

(looks up, a hint of vulnerability in her eyes) I'm also scared of feeling like I'm failing, like I'm not good enough or something. It's like, I'll make a mistake or something, and then I'll feel this huge sense of shame and guilt. And I don't know how to deal with it, so I just...numb myself, like I said.

(pauses, looking down) But I think I need to feel safe, you know? Like, I need to feel like I'm not going to fall apart or something. And I need to feel like I'm not alone, that someone is here to support me. (looks up, a small smile on her face) I guess that's why I'm here, right? To feel safe and supported, even when the feelings are intense?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Yes. Exactly. You’re here because you *deserve* to feel safe and supported—not just when things are easy, but especially when they’re hard. And what you just shared? That’s not weakness. That’s courage. You’re naming the things that scare you most, and that’s the first step toward taking their power away.

Those feelings—anxiety, sadness, shame—they’re heavy, and it makes sense that you’d want to escape them. But here’s what I want you to know: you’re already carrying them, even when you numb. The difference is that when you numb, you’re carrying them *alone*. When you face them, even just a little at a time, you don’t have to carry them by yourself. That’s what we’re doing here. That’s what therapy is for.

You mentioned shame—that feeling of "I’m not good enough." Shame thrives in secrecy and silence. But the moment you speak it out loud, like you just did, it starts to lose its grip. It’s like turning on a light in a dark room. The fear doesn’t disappear, but it doesn’t feel so all-consuming anymore.

So let’s start small. When that anxiety or sadness or shame starts to feel like too much, what’s one tiny thing you could do to remind yourself that you’re safe in that moment? Maybe it’s grounding yourself by naming things you can see or touch, or reaching out to someone who gets it. Maybe it’s just taking a deep breath and saying, *"This feels big, but I don’t have to fix it all right now."*

You don’t have to do this perfectly. You just have to be willing to try. And I’m right here with you. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text:
(looks down, a small smile on her face) That sounds...like a relief, actually. Like, I don’t have to have all the answers or fix everything right now. I just have to...show up, I guess. (looks up, meeting the therapist's eyes) And be willing to try, like you said.

(pauses, taking a deep breath) Yeah, I think I can do that. I can try to face these feelings, even if it’s just a little at a time. And I can remind myself that I’m safe, that I don’t have to carry this alone. (smiles slightly) And it feels...good, actually. Like, it feels like I can finally start to let go of some of this weight I've been carrying around.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I’m so glad you’re feeling that sense of relief—it’s a sign that you’re already starting to shift how you relate to these feelings. You’re right: you don’t have to fix everything right now. You just have to show up, be willing, and take it one step at a time. That’s not just progress; that’s *strength*.

The fact that you’re already feeling some of that weight lift just by talking about it? That’s proof that you *can* handle these feelings, even if it’s hard. They don’t have to control you. You’re learning that you can face them without falling apart, and that’s huge.

So let’s celebrate this moment. You’re choosing to trust yourself, to trust this process, and to trust that you’re not alone in it. That’s brave. And I’m here to remind you: you don’t have to do this perfectly. You just have to keep showing up.

What’s one small thing you’d like to try this week to remind yourself that you’re safe, even when the feelings feel big? Maybe it’s a grounding technique, or reaching out to someone when you’re struggling, or even just giving yourself permission to pause and breathe. What feels doable for you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiles, feeling a sense of hope and determination) I think I'd like to try writing down how I'm feeling when I'm overwhelmed. Just to get it out of my head and onto paper, I guess. And then maybe...maybe I can look at it later and see that it's not as big as it felt in the moment. (looks up, meeting the therapist's eyes) Does that sound like a good place to start?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That sounds like an *excellent* place to start. Writing can be such a powerful tool because it gives you a way to externalize those overwhelming feelings—to take them out of your head and put them somewhere else, where you can look at them without them feeling so all-consuming. It’s like creating a little distance between you and the emotion, which can make it feel more manageable.

And you’re absolutely right: when you look back at what you’ve written later, you might start to notice patterns or realize that the feelings aren’t as permanent or as big as they felt in the moment. That’s the beauty of it—it helps you see that emotions are temporary, even when they feel overwhelming in the moment.

Would you like to try a little exercise now to practice this? You don’t have to share it with me if you don’t want to, but it might help to get a sense of how it feels. You could start by just writing down one thing you’re feeling right now, in this moment. It could be as simple as, *"I feel hopeful, but also a little nervous about trying this."* Or it could be something bigger. There’s no right or wrong way to do it—just let it flow.

How does that sound? Would you like to give it a try?
